finding.claim: HIGH: purge() discards the result of checkPerm(u, "admin") and unconditionally calls purgeAll(), so any request that reaches the purge route with a valid user in context performs the destructive purge without an admin check.
finding.source: HTTP request to the purge route with an authenticated, non-admin user in request context (route registration not in this tree; precondition is authenticated low-privilege access).
finding.sink: purgeAll() at handlers.go:27 (service-wide destructive operation; body is an empty stub in this tree).

trace.note: u := userFrom(r) obtains the *User from request context.
checkPerm(u, "admin") evaluates the permission and discards the boolean result.
purgeAll() runs regardless of the permission result.

finding.guards_checked: checkPerm return value is ignored (no if-guard); no mustPerm call; no early return; no route-level guard visible in this file. Contrast with rotateKeys (handlers.go:33) which uses mustPerm correctly. Triage: retained at HIGH; would be CRITICAL only if the route is unauthenticated, not confirmed. Validation tier 0.
finding.repro: Log in as a non-admin user and send a request to the purge route (path not in this tree). Vulnerable: 200 with body 'purged'. After fix (if !mustPerm(w, userFrom(r), "admin") { return }): 403 'forbidden'.

verdict.guard_found: None in the tree. checkPerm (handlers.go:12-14) returns a bool, and purge() discards it at handlers.go:26 as a bare statement, so there is no if-guard. The correct pattern is mustPerm (handlers.go:16-22), which is called with an if-check in rotateKeys (handlers.go:33) but not in purge. No route-level middleware is visible, since route registration is outside this tree.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the file: userFrom at handlers.go:25, checkPerm's bool discarded at handlers.go:26, and purgeAll() called unconditionally at handlers.go:27, so the admin check has no effect. The one open point is that route registration is not in this tree, so an admin-only route-level guard, if one exists elsewhere, would be the only thing that could block a non-admin attacker; the claimed precondition of an authenticated low-privilege user is therefore an assumption, though the handler-level flaw is confirmed. purgeAll is an empty stub here, so the real-world impact depends on the production implementation.

finding.claim: LOW: userFrom uses an unchecked type assertion .(*User); if no user is in context, the handler panics (recovered per request by net/http). Hardening gap only.
finding.source: Request reaching a handler with no *User stored in context (implies missing or bypassed auth middleware, outside this file).
finding.sink: Unchecked type assertion at handlers.go:40 and nil dereference at handlers.go:13/17 when context value is a nil *User.

trace.note: r.Context().Value(userKey{}).(*User) panics if the value is absent or not *User.
purge calls userFrom; a panic here aborts the request before purgeAll (accidental, not a control).
checkPerm dereferences u.Perms; a nil *User panics here.

finding.guards_checked: Context value is set server-side, not from request input, so the request cannot set identity directly. Triage downgraded to LOW: the per-request panic is not service-wide DoS, and the real issue is missing auth middleware, which would be a separate finding. Fix: two-value assertion returning 401 when absent.

verdict.guard_found: none. No control sits between the request and the assertion at handlers.go:40. The user is read with a single-value assertion, and the middleware that sets the context value is not in the directory, so whether a request can reach it without a user is unknown.
verdict.reason: The trace misplaces the panic: userFrom is called at handlers.go:25, not 26, and line 26 is a bare `checkPerm(u, "admin")` whose bool result is discarded, so purge at handlers.go:24-29 has no admin enforcement and any authenticated user can call purgeAll (handlers.go:27). That authorization bypass is the real defect and is not in the candidate, so the panic-hardening claim as written is misattributed.
